newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court says bank can close Scientology accounts.
newsitem.headline: German court says bank can close Scientology accounts.

text.p: A German high court on Friday lifted an injunction preventing the state-owned German post office savings bank, Deutsche Postbank AG, from closing accounts held by the Scientology organisation.

The bank had argued it had the right to choose its own customers. "We did not want to be associated to a group which is regarded by the public as a criminal organisation", spokesman Werner Merkes said.
Hans-Juergen Voigt, presiding judge at the Stuttgart court in southern Germany, ruled that Scientology had enough alternatives in finding somewhere to place its accounts.

He said Postbank, which is due to be sold off by the government as part of the break-up of the postal monopoly, had no obligation to accept all comers as account-holders since it became a joint stock company last year.
The bank's Ulm branch had closed Scientology's accounts with immediate effect in July. The accounts had been run in accordance with the bank's regulations.

Scientology said the court decision was the result of a "cynical propaganda campaign" and that it was the target of a "systematic policy of discrimination which aims radically to exclude Scientology members and their community from society and economy". The group said it would appeal.
The organisation sees itself as the victim of a campaign sanctioned by German Labour Minister Norbert Bluem and Family Affairs Minister Claudia Nolte.
Both have argued Scientology is a commercial organisation and should be denied its current status as a religious grouping.

The Young Union, the youth organisation of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, angered Scientology by calling for a boycott of the box-office hit movie Mission Impossible because its star, Tom Cruise, is a Scientologist.
